title: Linear Equations in One Variable, Part 1: The Idea and an Easy Problem

beats.say: A linear equation in one variable has a single unknown number, usually called x. The unknown is never squared, never under a square root, and never in a denominator.
You solve it by undoing operations, one at a time, until x stands alone on one side of the equals sign. The goal is always x equals a number.

card.text: Undo operations until x is alone

beats.say: The SAT asks three kinds of questions about these equations. You may need to solve one, build one from a short story, or decide how many solutions it has.

card.text: Solve it, build it, count solutions

beats.say: First, whatever you do to one side of the equation, you must do to the other side. That keeps both sides equal, and it's the reason every step in this video is allowed.
beats.item: Do the same to both sides

beats.say: Second, distribute first. Multiply the number outside the parentheses by every term inside, then combine like terms on each side, then move all the x terms to one side.
Third, clear fractions early. Multiply every term on both sides by the least common denominator. Decimals work the same way, by multiplying by ten or one hundred.
Fourth, in a word problem, a one-time amount is a constant, and a per-unit amount multiplies the variable. A twenty dollar fee plus eight dollars per hour becomes twenty plus eight h.
Picture an equation as a balance scale. On the left is x plus three small blocks, and on the right are seven small blocks. The scale is level, so both sides weigh the same.
If we take blocks away from only one side, the scale tips, and the two sides are no longer equal. So changing just one side of an equation isn't allowed.
But if we do the same thing to both sides, the scale stays level. That's the golden rule of solving equations.
Let's take three blocks away from both sides. The left side has x alone, and the right side has four blocks.
The scale is still level, which tells us that x weighs the same as four blocks. In other words, x equals four.
Here's that scale written as an equation, x plus three equals seven. We want x alone, so we need to get rid of the plus three.
Subtract three from both sides. On the left, the three cancels, leaving x. On the right, seven minus three is four.
Distributing a negative flips every sign inside the parentheses. For example, negative two times the quantity x minus three equals negative two x plus six.
beats.item: A negative outside flips every sign

beats.say: To clear fractions, multiply by the least common denominator. For x over four and x over six, multiply by twelve, because twelve is the smallest number both denominators divide into.
beats.item: Multiply by the least common denominator

beats.say: After simplifying, every linear equation can be written as a x plus b equals c x plus d. Comparing the coefficients tells you how many solutions there are.
beats.item: Every equation looks like ax + b = cx + d

beats.say: Now an easy example. Solve seven x plus four equals three x plus twenty-four. There are x terms on both sides, so our plan is to collect them on one side first.
We have seven x on the left and three x on the right. Our plan has three steps: move the x terms together, move the plain numbers together, and then divide.
First, subtract three x from both sides. We do this because we want all the x terms on the left. Three x minus three x is zero, so that term disappears from the right.
Next, subtract four from both sides. This removes the plain number from the left, so only the x term remains there. Twenty-four minus four is twenty.
Finally, divide both sides by four. Four x divided by four is x, and twenty divided by four is five. So x equals five.
Always check by putting five back into the original equation. On the left, seven times five plus four is thirty-nine. On the right, three times five plus twenty-four is also thirty-nine.
To recap. A linear equation in one variable has one unknown, and we solve it by undoing operations until x is alone.
beats.item: Undo operations until x is alone

beats.say: Whatever we do to one side, we do to the other, and we always distribute first, collect the x terms, and then divide.
beats.item: Same to both sides, distribute first

beats.say: Always check the answer by substituting. In the next video, we work through a medium problem and a hard problem.
